mcqs.question: What is a 'thread' in Java?

options.B: A lightweight unit of execution within a process that can run concurrently with other threads
options.D: A database connection

mcqs.explanation: A thread is the smallest unit of execution. A Java program can have multiple threads running concurrently within the same process, sharing memory but having their own stack and execution path.

mcqs.question: What is multithreading?

options.B: Running multiple programs simultaneously
options.C: Concurrent execution of multiple threads within a single program
options.D: Using multiple monitors

mcqs.explanation: Multithreading allows a single program to perform multiple tasks concurrently. Each thread executes independently but can share data. This improves resource utilization and enables responsive applications.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is one way to create a thread in Java?

options.B: Extend the Process class
options.D: Extend the Runnable class

mcqs.explanation: There are two main ways to create a thread: 1) Extend the Thread class and override run(), 2) Implement the Runnable interface and pass it to a Thread object. Both are valid approaches.

mcqs.question: What method contains the code that the thread will execute?

options.B: execute()
options.D: start()

mcqs.explanation: The run() method contains the code that executes in the new thread. You override run() in your Thread subclass or Runnable implementation to define the thread's work.

mcqs.question: How do you START a thread in Java?

options.A: Call run() on the Thread object
options.B: Call start() on the Thread object
options.C: Call execute() on the Thread object
options.D: Call launch() on the Thread object

mcqs.explanation: Call start() to begin thread execution. start() allocates a new OS thread and calls run() in that new thread. Calling run() directly executes in the current thread — no new thread is created.

mcqs.question: What is the initial state of a Thread object before start() is called?

options.B: Blocked
options.D: Dead

mcqs.explanation: A Thread object that has been created (new Thread()) but not yet started is in the 'New' state. It transitions to 'Runnable' when start() is called, then to 'Running' when the scheduler gives it CPU time.

mcqs.question: What are the benefits of multithreading?

options.B: Better CPU utilization, responsive UIs, parallel computation, faster I/O handling
options.D: Eliminates the need for synchronization

mcqs.explanation: Multithreading benefits: better CPU utilization (computation while waiting for I/O), responsive UIs (UI thread stays active while background work happens), faster computation on multi-core processors, and efficient handling of multiple network requests.

mcqs.question: What is 'concurrency' in the context of multithreading?

options.A: Threads executing sequentially one after another
options.B: Multiple threads making progress, potentially overlapping in time (interleaving or true parallelism)
options.D: Synchronized access to shared data

mcqs.explanation: Concurrency means multiple threads are making progress at the same time — either interleaved on one CPU or truly parallel on multi-core. Concurrent programs can complete more work in the same time but require careful coordination to avoid data corruption.

mcqs.question: What does Thread.sleep(1000) do?

options.B: Pauses the current thread for 1000 milliseconds
options.C: Runs the thread for exactly 1000 milliseconds
options.D: Creates a delay in the main program only

mcqs.explanation: Thread.sleep(ms) pauses the CURRENT thread for the specified number of milliseconds, temporarily releasing CPU. Other threads can run during this time. It throws InterruptedException which must be handled or declared.

mcqs.question: What is a 'race condition'?

options.A: A competition between threads for CPU time
options.B: Unpredictable results when multiple threads access shared data simultaneously without synchronization
options.C: A thread running faster than expected
options.D: Memory corruption due to large arrays

mcqs.explanation: A race condition occurs when the result depends on the timing of thread execution. Two threads reading and writing the same variable without synchronization can produce inconsistent, unpredictable results — sometimes correct, sometimes wrong.

mcqs.question: What is the difference between calling run() directly vs calling start() on a Thread?

options.A: No difference — both create a new thread
options.B: start() creates a new OS thread and invokes run() in it; calling run() directly executes in the calling thread — no new thread is created
options.D: start() must be called twice to actually start the thread

mcqs.explanation: This is a critical distinction. t.run() calls run() in the current thread — exactly like a regular method call, no concurrency. t.start() creates a new OS-level thread that independently calls run(). Always use start() for concurrent execution.

mcqs.question: What is the second way to create a thread (besides extending Thread)?

options.B: Implementing the Runnable interface and passing the object to a Thread constructor
options.D: Implementing Callable and using Thread directly

mcqs.explanation: Implementing Runnable: class MyTask implements Runnable { public void run() { ... } }. Then: Thread t = new Thread(new MyTask()); t.start(). This is preferred when your class must extend another class (Java single inheritance).

mcqs.question: Why is implementing Runnable preferred over extending Thread in most cases?

options.B: Because Java has single inheritance — implementing Runnable allows your class to still extend another class if needed
options.D: Thread class is deprecated

mcqs.explanation: Java allows only single inheritance. If your task class extends Thread, it cannot extend any other class. Implementing Runnable separates the task (what to do) from the execution mechanism (Thread), following separation of concerns and allowing inheritance flexibility.

mcqs.question: What are the five states in the Java Thread lifecycle?

options.B: New, Runnable, Running, Blocked/Waiting, Terminated
options.D: Pending, Active, Waiting, Locked, Dead

mcqs.explanation: Thread lifecycle: New (created, not started) → Runnable (start() called, waiting for CPU) → Running (CPU assigned, run() executing) → Blocked/Waiting (waiting for lock, I/O, or sleep()) → Terminated (run() completed or exception). The thread scheduler manages transitions.

mcqs.question: What does the 'synchronized' keyword do in Java?

options.A: Makes the method run synchronously in sequence
options.B: Acquires a lock before executing, ensuring only one thread can execute that block/method at a time
options.D: Prevents the thread from being interrupted

mcqs.explanation: synchronized ensures mutual exclusion. Only one thread can hold a given object's lock at a time. Other threads trying to enter a synchronized block/method on the same object will block until the lock is released. Prevents race conditions on shared data.

mcqs.question: What is a 'deadlock' in multithreading?

options.B: Two or more threads each waiting for the other to release a lock, causing permanent standstill
options.C: A thread sleeping for too long
options.D: CPU overload from too many threads

mcqs.explanation: Deadlock: Thread A holds Lock1 and waits for Lock2; Thread B holds Lock2 and waits for Lock1. Neither can proceed. Deadlock is prevented by: always acquiring locks in the same order, using tryLock() with timeout, or minimizing lock scope.

mcqs.question: What is Thread priority in Java?

options.A: The order in which threads are created
options.B: A hint to the thread scheduler about the relative importance of a thread; ranges from MIN_PRIORITY(1) to MAX_PRIORITY(10)
options.C: The CPU core assigned to the thread
options.D: The memory priority for the thread

mcqs.explanation: Thread priority (1-10) is a hint (not a guarantee) to the scheduler. Higher-priority threads are more likely to get CPU time. NORM_PRIORITY=5 is default. t.setPriority(Thread.MAX_PRIORITY) sets priority 10. Actual scheduling is OS-dependent.

mcqs.question: What does thread.join() do?

options.B: Makes the current thread wait until the specified thread completes execution
options.C: Adds the thread to a pool
options.D: Starts the thread

mcqs.explanation: thread.join() causes the calling thread to wait until 'thread' finishes. main() calling t.join() will wait for thread t to complete before continuing. Useful for ensuring one thread's results are available before another continues.

mcqs.question: What is the producer-consumer problem in multithreading?

options.A: A problem with file reading and writing speeds
options.B: A classic synchronization problem where one thread produces data and another consumes it — they must coordinate to avoid buffer overflow/underflow
options.D: A problem with database read/write conflicts

mcqs.explanation: Producer-Consumer: a producer thread generates items and puts them in a buffer; a consumer thread takes items from the buffer. Coordination is needed: consumer must wait if buffer is empty; producer must wait if buffer is full. Solved using wait(), notify(), or BlockingQueue.

mcqs.question: How does multithreading improve the performance of a web server?

options.B: Each client request is handled by a separate thread, allowing multiple clients to be served concurrently instead of sequentially
options.D: Web servers don't use Java threads

mcqs.explanation: Without multithreading, a web server processes requests one at a time — client 2 waits while client 1 is served. With multithreading, each client gets its own thread, enabling concurrent processing of hundreds of clients. This is fundamental to Java's use in enterprise web servers (Tomcat, Jetty).

mcqs.question: Why does calling run() directly instead of start() NOT create concurrent execution, even though run() contains the task code?

options.B: start() registers the thread with the JVM thread scheduler; run() is just a regular instance method — calling it directly just executes in the caller's thread stack, no new OS thread is allocated
options.C: run() uses a different CPU core automatically
options.D: Only start() can access the Thread class's run() method

mcqs.explanation: Threads are OS-level resources. Thread.start() makes a JVM native call to create a new OS thread, register it with the scheduler, and have that new thread call run(). t.run() is syntactically identical to any other method call — it executes in the calling thread's stack with no concurrency or separate stack allocation.

mcqs.question: What is the 'volatile' keyword and when should it be used instead of 'synchronized'?

options.B: volatile guarantees visibility of changes across threads (no caching); use it for simple flags/counters where atomicity of a single read/write is sufficient, not for compound check-then-act operations
options.C: volatile is faster than synchronized always
options.D: volatile prevents deadlocks

mcqs.explanation: Without volatile, threads may cache variable values locally — changes by one thread are invisible to others. volatile forces reads/writes to go to main memory. Use volatile for simple flags (boolean running = false) where visibility matters. For compound operations (check-then-act), volatile is insufficient — use synchronized or AtomicInteger.

mcqs.question: What is the difference between thread-safety via 'synchronized' and using 'java.util.concurrent.atomic' classes like AtomicInteger?

options.A: No difference — both provide identical guarantees
options.B: synchronized uses OS-level locking (blocking); AtomicInteger uses CPU compare-and-swap (CAS) hardware instructions (non-blocking, lower overhead for simple operations)
options.D: Atomic classes require external libraries

mcqs.explanation: synchronized acquires an OS mutex — if the lock is held, other threads block. AtomicInteger uses CAS (hardware-level compare-and-swap) which is non-blocking: if the CAS fails, it retries in a loop ('spin lock'). For simple counters/flags, atomic classes have lower overhead than synchronized; for complex multi-step operations, synchronized is needed.

mcqs.question: If two threads T1 and T2 both increment a shared counter 1000 times each without synchronization, what is the likely final value and why?

options.B: Less than 2000 — because increment is read-modify-write (3 steps), multiple threads can read the same value before either writes back, losing increments
options.D: Exactly 1000 — only one thread's work survives

mcqs.explanation: counter++ is NOT atomic — it's three operations: READ counter, ADD 1, WRITE counter. If T1 reads 500 and T2 reads 500 (before either writes), both write 501, losing one increment. This race condition means the final value is 2000 only if perfectly interleaved. In practice, it's less than 2000 and non-deterministic.

mcqs.question: What is 'thread starvation' and how does it differ from deadlock?

options.B: In deadlock, threads wait forever for each other (circular dependency); in starvation, a thread is perpetually denied CPU time because higher-priority threads always preempt it
options.C: Starvation involves disk I/O; deadlock involves network
options.D: Deadlock is recoverable; starvation is not

mcqs.explanation: Deadlock: threads form a cycle of lock dependencies — no one can proceed. Starvation: one thread can proceed but never gets scheduled because others always take priority. Starvation can be solved by priority aging (gradually increasing thread priority the longer it waits) or fair locks (ReentrantLock(true) in Java).

mcqs.question: What is the memory consistency guarantee of the 'happens-before' relationship in Java's memory model?

options.A: Actions happen in the order they are coded
options.B: If action A 'happens-before' action B, all changes made by A are visible to B — establishing a consistent view of shared memory between threads
options.C: Memory is allocated before code executes
options.D: Thread A always completes before Thread B

mcqs.explanation: Java Memory Model defines 'happens-before': if unlock happens-before lock on same monitor, the thread that unlocks's writes are visible to the thread that locks. Thread.start() happens-before any action in the started thread. These guarantees allow safe publication of data between threads without explicit volatile/synchronized everywhere.

mcqs.question: Why is creating too many threads (thread-per-task model for thousands of tasks) problematic?

options.A: Java doesn't allow more than 100 threads
options.B: Each thread consumes OS resources (stack memory ~1MB, OS structures); thousands of threads thrash the scheduler and exhaust memory
options.C: More threads always means worse performance
options.D: Threads cannot share data if there are too many

mcqs.explanation: Each Java thread maps to an OS thread with ~1MB default stack. 1000 threads = ~1GB just for stacks. OS scheduling overhead becomes significant with many threads. Modern Java uses thread pools (Executors) or virtual threads (Java 19+) to reuse a small number of OS threads for large numbers of concurrent tasks.

mcqs.question: What is the difference between 'wait()' and 'sleep()' in Java threads?

options.B: sleep() pauses the thread for a time without releasing locks; wait() releases the lock on the object and waits until notify() wakes it — used for inter-thread coordination
options.C: wait() is for I/O; sleep() is for computation
options.D: sleep() can only be called from synchronized blocks

mcqs.explanation: sleep(ms) pauses but HOLDS all locks — other threads cannot enter synchronized blocks on those objects. wait() must be called from a synchronized block, RELEASES the monitor lock (allowing other threads to enter), and blocks until notify()/notifyAll() wakes it. wait() is for inter-thread communication; sleep() is for time-based delays.

mcqs.question: What problem does 'ThreadLocal' solve in multithreaded Java applications?

options.B: Providing each thread with its own independent copy of a variable, avoiding synchronization for per-thread state (e.g., per-request database connection, user session)
options.D: Automatically synchronizing access to collections

mcqs.explanation: ThreadLocal<T> gives each thread its own isolated copy of a variable. get()/set() operate on the current thread's copy. Example: ThreadLocal<Connection> — each request thread has its own database connection without synchronization overhead. Spring's @Transactional uses ThreadLocal to bind connections to threads.

mcqs.question: How does Java's fork/join framework (java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool) differ from traditional thread pools?

options.A: Fork/join is only for GUI applications
options.B: Fork/join implements work-stealing: idle worker threads steal tasks from busy workers' queues, optimizing CPU utilization for recursive divide-and-conquer tasks
options.C: Fork/join creates more threads than traditional pools
options.D: Fork/join is single-threaded internally

mcqs.explanation: Traditional thread pools: fixed worker threads take tasks from a shared queue. Fork/join: each worker has its own deque; when empty, it steals tasks from other workers' deques (work-stealing). This is highly efficient for recursive algorithms (merge sort, tree traversal) where tasks divide into subtasks unevenly. Used internally by Java 8+ parallel streams.
